newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to set 2000 horizon for Hungary's EU entry.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to set 2000 horizon for Hungary's EU entry.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, flanked by top French business executives, will tell Hungary on Thursday that France hopes it will join the European Union in 2000.

"The president will reply unambiguously and positively to the two questions which many Hungarians are asking: France warmly supports Hungary's entry into the European Union and the same goes for its membership of a renovated Atlantic Alliance," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told reporters.
As with his visit to Poland last September, he will tell parliament in Budapest at the start of his two-day visit that Paris "aims for the year 2000" for Hungary's EU accession.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, accompanying Chirac, will travel on immediately to Prague to convey the same message of support to the Czech Republic ahead of a presidential visit there later in the year.
European Commission experts have said that deadline is unrealistic and it will probably take at least two years longer for the first former Communist Central European states to join.
But Colonna said: "It is possible if, as we hope, the intergovernmental conference (on reforming EU institutions) does not run late, and if things are well prepared. But that does not depend on us."

Diplomats said Chirac was anxious to erase the negative image of France created across Central and Eastern Europe by his predecessor Francois Mitterrand's statement after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 in which he said that it would be "decades" before the first former Communist states joined the EU.

That statement, and early French resistance to removing barriers to imports especially of farm produce from those countries, cast Paris in the eyes of many east Europeans as the main adversary of their entry into the EU "rich men's club".

It may also have limited the enthusiasm of French companies for investing in the area's emerging markets. Although Budapest receives half of all French investment in Central and Eastern Europe, Paris was only Hungary's fifth supplier in 1995 with four percent of market share, according to official figures.

A dozen top industrialists will accompany the president, including the chairmen of state electricity and gas companies EDF and GDF, missiles and electronics firm Matra, construction giant Bouygues and utilities company Lyonnaise des Eaux.
Colonna said the conservative Chirac considered Hungary was one of the countries which had prepared itself best for membership through economic reform and cooperation with NATO.

Budapest received some 600 million European currency units ($732 million) in EU aid between 1990 and 1995 for some 60 modernisation projects and it is due to get a further 485 million Ecus ($592 million) in the period 1995-1999.
The other major issue in talks with President Arpad Gonzc and Prime Minister Gyla Horn will be Hungary's bid for NATO membership, which Colonna said France supported unreservedly.

She said Chirac would set out his vision of a future cooperative European security architecture founded on a new relationship between the Atlantic Alliance and Russia, which has bitterly opposed NATO expansion plans.

The president will praise Hungary's decisive role in lifting the Iron Curtain in 1989 and decorate about a dozen figures who distinguished themselves in the 1956 anti-Soviet Hungarian uprising with France's Legion d'Honneur medal.
